source.title_on_document: GenAI-driven storytelling on senior secondary students' Generative AI literacy and writing skills: A mixed-methods research

supplement.holds: The paper refers to no supplement or online appendix. No tables of means, SDs, test statistics, ANCOVA results, or Cohen's d appear anywhere, although Section 3.6 says ANCOVA and Cohen's d were computed.

paper_design_summary: 76 Form 4 and Form 5 students at one Band 3 secondary school in Hong Kong were assigned (the paper says by simple random sampling) to a five-week, ten-hour GenAI-driven digital storytelling workshop (n = 38) or to conventional English lessons without AI (n = 38). Before and after the intervention, both groups wrote a storytelling task without AI help, scored with the Carey et al. (2022) creative writing rubric on word usage, narrative structure, and creativity (total out of 15), and completed self-report AI literacy and writing anxiety questionnaires; nine experimental students were interviewed.

studies.label: Classroom experiment: GenAI storytelling workshop vs conventional English lessons (Hong Kong secondary school)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Five-week, ten-hour GenAI-driven storytelling workshop (experimental) vs conventional English lessons without exposure to AI tools (control)
assignment.quote: Participants were assigned to either the experimental or control group through a process of simple random sampling.
assignment.locator: PDF p. 6 (journal p. 84), Section 3.3; also abstract PDF p. 1 (p. 79): "76 students who were randomly assigned to control and experimental groups"

arms.name: Experimental (GenAI storytelling workshop)
arms.description: Five consecutive weeks, two 60-minute sessions per week in the school computer lab; 5-step GenAI storytelling model (AI concepts, prompt crafting and outlining with GenAI, GenAI visuals, AI music, final story editing and presentation); instructor-designed prompt banks and guided prompt examples

arms.name: Control (conventional English lessons)
arms.description: Continued with conventional English lessons without exposure to any AI tools

participants.exclusions: None reported. The paper never states how many students completed the post-test or entered each analysis; the 76 (38 per group) is the count given at grouping and repeated at the start of the Results section. The analyzed count is taken from that Results statement, not from an explicit analysis N.
participants.who: Form 4 and Form 5 (senior secondary) students at a government-funded Band 3 school in a public housing district serving socioeconomically disadvantaged students; experimental group 18 Form 4 and 20 Form 5
participants.quote: This study was conducted at a Band 3 secondary school in Hong Kong and involved a total of 76 students from Form 4 and Form 5.
participants.locator: PDF p. 5 (journal p. 83), Section 3.1; PDF p. 8 (p. 86), Section 4.1: "A total of 76 students were divided equally into experimental and control groups"; Figure 1, PDF p. 6 (p. 84): 38 students per group

ai_tool.name_model: Not named; the paper says "Gen AI tools" for text, visuals, and music
ai_tool.how_used: Multimodal digital storytelling workshop: students used GenAI for 5W1H brainstorming, prompt crafting and outline building, creating and revising visuals, generating AI music, and story editing, supported by instructor-designed prompt banks and guided prompt examples (Table 1, PDF p. 7; Section 3.2, PDF p. 6). AI was not available during the scored pre-test and post-test writing.

task.description: Storytelling (narrative writing) task done without AI help at pre-test and post-test, scored with the Creative Writing Assessment Rubric (Carey et al., 2022) on word usage, narrative structure, and creativity; total out of 15
task.duration: Intervention: five weeks, two 60-minute sessions per week (ten hours). Duration of the scored writing task: not stated.

outcomes.name: Creativity (rubric dimension) of post-test story written without AI
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Creativity dimension of the Creative Writing Assessment Rubric (Carey et al., 2022). The paper does not say who scored the writing samples, whether scorers were blind to group, or inter-rater reliability. Score range of this dimension not stated (total of three dimensions is out of 15).
outcomes.delay: Post-test administered immediately after the five-week intervention (Section 3.3, PDF p. 6)

contrasts.reported: No between-group statistic printed for creativity. Text: "Post-test results indicated higher writing scores for students in the experimental group"; "the control group did not show statistically significant changes in overall writing performance ... across any measured dimension". No control-group means are shown. ANCOVA and Cohen's d are described in Methods but no results are printed.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 11 (journal p. 89), RQ3 text; PDF p. 8 (p. 86), Section 3.6

contrasts.reported: Figure 3 bars only (no printed values): creativity pre-test about 1, post-test about 2.7 (read from figure, approximate). Text: "significant gains across all assessed writing skill dimensions in the experimental group"; no test statistic or p-value printed for writing dimensions.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 12 (journal p. 90), Figure 3; PDF p. 11 (p. 89), RQ3 Findings

outcomes.name: Total writing score (out of 15) of post-test story written without AI
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Sum of the three rubric dimensions (word usage, narrative structure, creativity) of the Carey et al. (2022) Creative Writing Assessment Rubric, out of 15. Overall writing quality including creativity. Scorer not stated.
outcomes.delay: Post-test administered immediately after the five-week intervention

contrasts.reported: No between-group statistic printed. Text says the control group "did not show statistically significant changes in overall writing performance"; no control means given.
"The mean overall writing score increased from 3.34 to 8.71 out of 15." (experimental group). No SD, n, test statistic, or p-value printed.

outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Narrative structure dimension of the Carey et al. (2022) rubric (a quality dimension; could be read as usefulness/quality). Scorer not stated.

outcomes.question: after_ai

eligibility.reason: The paper states that the 76 students were randomly assigned to a GenAI storytelling workshop or to conventional English lessons without AI (abstract, PDF p. 1; Section 3.3, PDF p. 6), 38 per arm, and scores creativity on stories written without AI help at post-test (Figure 1, PDF p. 6). Caveats: the same section calls the design a "pretest-posttest quasi-experimental design" and describes assignment as "simple random sampling", so the randomization claim is thinly documented; the unit of assignment (student vs class) is not stated explicitly; no between-group statistics are printed, only experimental pre/post figure bars and one text mean (3.34 to 8.71 of 15). The outcome is after_ai.

one_line_finding: In 76 Hong Kong secondary students, the GenAI storytelling group's no-AI post-test writing score rose from 3.34 to 8.71 out of 15 with gains in rubric-rated creativity (Figure 3, PDF p. 12; text p. 89), while the control is said to show no significant change; no between-group statistics are printed.
open_questions: Random assignment: the abstract says "randomly assigned" and Section 3.3 says "simple random sampling", but the same section calls the design "quasi-experimental". Was assignment truly random and at the student level, or by class?

No control-group writing means and no between-group test, ANCOVA result, or Cohen's d are printed, although Section 3.6 says ANCOVA and Cohen's d were computed. Extraction of a between-arm effect would need the author.
Who scored the writing samples (the author-teacher or independent raters), whether scoring was blind to group, and inter-rater reliability are not stated.
The number of students who completed the post-test is not stated; no attrition is reported.

The control group's post-test was also a no-AI storytelling task, but the control received conventional English lessons rather than an equivalent writing workshop, so the contrast mixes the GenAI tool with ten hours of a dedicated storytelling workshop.
notes: Section numbering in the PDF skips from 3.3.2 to 3.6. Outcomes not listed because they are self-reports, not scored on output: AI literacy questionnaire (affective, behavioral, cognitive, ethical; Figure 2, PDF p. 10, experimental pre/post only, p < .001 within group) and Writing Anxiety Scale (Cheng, 2004; somatic, avoidance, cognitive; Figure 4, PDF p. 13, experimental pre/post only, p < .001). Qualitative interviews with 9 experimental students (Figure 1). Construct coding: word usage, narrative structure, and total score are coded "other"; they are rubric quality dimensions and could alternatively be coded "usefulness". The measure field is "not_stated" because the paper never says who scored the rubric; human scoring by a rubric is implied but the rater type is not given. Figure 3 values in "reported" are approximate readings of unlabeled bars, not printed numbers; only the total (3.34 to 8.71) is printed in text. Figure 3 caption says "Experimental Group" only; the control group's writing scores appear nowhere. The author is a secondary school English teacher in Hong Kong (PDF p. 17); the paper does not say whether he taught the participants.
